editorial_title_zh: Deadline 评选本周院线新片：《纽约唯一的活扒手》、《温柔怪兽》、《海之女王》等
editorial_excerpt_zh: 本周的院线新片继续向电影颁奖季迈进，那些最早在圣丹斯等电影节上以极高声誉亮相的影片也开始登陆美国银幕。Deadline 汇总了我们全年评测过并即将上映的电影……

article_text:
This week’s theatrical releases continue the march into movie awards season, with the emergence on U.S. screens of films that started their journeys with buzzy festival launches as far back as Sundance.

Deadline has compiled its list of movies we’ve reviewed across the year that are now hitting cinemas.

This week, that includes Sony Pictures Classics’ The Only Living Pickpocket in New York , which bowed at Sundance and just this week earned star John Turturro a Gotham Award nomination . Also, the Berlin Film Festival award winner Queen at Sea , a family drama featuring the powerful 1-2 punch of Juliette Binoche and Tom Courtenay.

RELATED: 53 Of The Most Anticipated Movies Of 2026 A pair of Netflix movies are also hitting screens before their streaming dates: Léa Seydoux in the Cannes pic Gentle Monster, and Peter Berg’s WWII pic The Mosquito Bowl which just world premiered at AFI Fest.

Scroll down to find Deadline’s reviews.

Friday, October 30 Wide releases Christmas at the Kringles Everest: The Other Side The Mongoose The Only Living Pickpocket in New York Limited releases The Canvas The Mosquito Bowl Once Upon a Time in… Hollywood (Re-release) Paging Hezbollah Queen at Sea Tad and the Magic Lamp Who Killed Alex Odeh?

‘The Only Living Pickpocket In New York’ Image Credit: MRC Release: Wide (October 30) Distributor: Sony Pictures Classics Director-screenwriter: Noah Segan Cast: John Turturro, Steve Buscemi, Giancarlo Esposito, Will Price, Tatiana Maslany Original review date: January 27 (Sundance Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: John Turturro’s Harry is a throwback, and so is this movie, a modest but really rather mesmerizing and forlorn film, one that’s curated just as much as it is directed. It’s about things past, about things gone, but also things that won’t stay dead as much as society wants that to happen. It’s also a film about vanishing bohemia, and it’s no coincidence many of the film’s storied leads are played by leading lights of New York’s iconic indie movie scene. — DW RELATED: ‘The Only Living Pickpocket In New York’ Review: John Turturro Steals The Show In Noah Segan’s Mesmerizing Debut – Sundance Film Festival

‘Gentle Monster’ Image Credit: Frédéric Batier/Netflix Release: Limited (October 30) Distributor: Netflix Director-screenwriter: Marie Kreutzer Cast: Léa Seydoux, Laurence Rupp, Jella Haase, Catherine Deneuve Original review date: May 15 (Cannes Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: Léa Seydoux gives a very committed, unaffected performance as an experimental pianist who must deal with the dawning knowledge that her beloved husband has a second life online as a pedophile pornographer in Marie Kreutzer’s measured fictional account of a family torn apart by similar accusations. — SB RELATED: ‘Gentle Monster’ Review: Léa Seydoux Gives A Committed Performance In Cluttered Story Of A Family Torn Apart – Cannes Film Festival

‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Image Credit: Netflix Release: Limited (October 30) Distributor: Netflix Director: Peter Berg Screenwriters: Peter Berg and Mark L. Smith Cast: Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson, Tom Francis, Brent Comer, Jack Ingram, Ella Newton, Peter Berg, Dominic Bogart, Lola Bond, Stacy Clausen, Billy Smith, Steven Sammut, Blake Erickson, Claudia Ware, Pat McAfee Original review date: October 23 (AFI Fest) Deadline’s takeaway: The Mosquito Bowl achieves its true strength by putting us directly into the center of the hell of war, a visceral experience so intense and unrelenting it seems we are there and, like those who were on the front lines, a feeling there is no way out. Fair warning: Peter Berg, whose films have included Lone Survivor, Deep Water Horizon and other tales of valor and courage against all odds, does not hold back in showing war’s true horrors. — PH RELATED: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: Peter Berg’s Powerful True WWII Story Takes Four Star Players From The Glory Of The Football Field To The Hell Of The Battlefield – AFI Fest

‘Queen At Sea’ Image Credit: Seafaring LLC Release: Limited (October 30) Distributor: Greenwich Entertainment Director-screenwriter: Lance Hammer Cast: Juliette Binoche, Tom Courtenay, Anna Calder-Marshall, Florence Hunt Original review date: February 19 (Berlin Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: The complications this particular family unit is facing are laid out starkly and without any further ado in Queen at Sea ‘s shocking opening moments. It’s a staggeringly bold gambit, but the two grounded, laser-focused leads — Juliette Binoche and Tom Courtenay — help navigate us through the intimate and surprisingly complex moral maze that unfolds. — DW RELATED: ‘Queen At Sea’ Review: Juliette Binoche And Tom Courtenay Light Up A Dark, Intimate Study Of Dementia – Berlin Film Festival

Friday, October 23 Wide releases Ali G: Who Iz I? Clayface Klara and the Sun A Talent for Murder Wicker Wildwood You Can See Everything Limited releases Fatherland Going for Two Human Kung Fu Soccer Little Thomas Love Language Possible Love Seniors Terrestrial 5 Centimeters Per Second

‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Image Credit: Amazon MGM Studios / Everett Collection Release: Wide (October 23) Distributor: Amazon MGM Studios Director: Sacha Baron Cohen Screenwriters: Sacha Baron Cohen & Anthony Hines & Peter Baynham & Dan Swimer & Dan Mazer & Keisha Zollar Cast: Sacha Baron Cohen, Morgana Robinson, Marion Robinson, Alphja Miknas, Clive Russell, Stewart Rodeheaver Review date: October 22 Deadline’s takeaway: Sacha Baron Cohen obviously believes the moment is right to bring back his LOL OG as the world has only sunk further into the abyss since his last appearance. While the new film drifts from bit to bit, some straining for laughs, enough of it works to make this feel like vintage Baron Cohen daredevil comedy at the expense of the clueless. — PH RELATED: ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Review: Sacha Baron Cohen’s Signature Prankster Returns In Outrageous Form With Something To Offend Everyone

‘Clayface’ Image Credit: Warner Bros./Courtesy Everett Collection Release: Wide (October 23) Distributor: Warner Bros/DC Studios Director: James Watkins Screenwriters: Mike Flanagan & Hossein Amini Cast: Tom Rhys Harries, Naomi Ackie, David Dencik, Max Minghella, Eddie Marsan Original review date: October 21 Deadline’s takeaway: Whether you’re a comic book nerd or a horror junkie, Clayface is worth the price of admission for its genre-driven approach to a lesser-known character, hopefully serving as a roadmap for the DCU’s onscreen future. Just maybe brace yourself if you’re squeamish. — GG RELATED: ‘Clayface’ Review: DCU Molds Batman Villain’s Origin Story Into Fun, Scary Body Horror

‘Klara And The Sun’ Image Credit: Sony / 3000 Pictures Release: Wide (October 23) Distributor: Sony Pictures Director: Taika Waititi Screenwriters: Taika Waititi and Dahvi Waller (based on the book by Kazuo Ishiguro) Cast: Jenna Ortega, Amy Adams, Mia Tharia, Natasha Lyonne, Aran Murphy, Steve Buscemi, Rachel House, Jesse Griffin Original review date: October 15 (London Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: Taiki Waititi should be a snug-as-a-bug fit for Kazuo Ishiguro’s dystopian — or is it? — 2021 novel, given the director’s affinity for a very particular and peculiar kind of reality-based cringe comedy. But Klara just doesn’t deliver on any of the fronts it promises. — DW RELATED: ‘Klara And The Sun’ Review: Taika Waititi’s Latest Is A Curiously Flat Dystopian Comedy-Drama – London Film Festival

‘Wicker’ Image Credit: Photo courtesy of Black Bear Release: Wide (October 23) Distributor: Black Bear Director-screenwriters: Alex Huston and Eleanor Wilson Cast: Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård, Peter Dinklage, Elizabeth Debicki, Richard E. Grant, Marli Siu, Nabhaan Rizwan, Gustav Lindh, Ella Bruccoleri, Ben Ashenden, Kiell Smith Binoe Original review date: October 22 Deadline’s takeaway: A hit at Sundance where it was picked up by Black Bear , this wry film from writer-directors Alex Huston and Eleanor Wilson is sexy and satirically funny, but also oddly haunting as a truly twisted fable that says its never too late to become your own best version of Cinderella. — PH RELATED: ‘Wicker’ Review: Olivia Colman And Peter Dinklage Turn Alexander Skarsgård Into A Sexy Basket Case In Comic Fable That’s Pure Delight

‘Wildwood’ Image Credit: Courtesy of Laika Release: Wide (October 23) Distributor: Fathom Director: Travis Knight Screenwriter: Chris Butler (based on the book by Colin Meloy) Cast: Carey Mulligan, Peyton Elizabeth Lee, Jacob Tremblay , Angela Bassett, Mahershala Ali, Awkwafina, Maya Erskine, Jake Johnson, Charlie Day, Tom Waits, Richard E. Grant, Amanda Stenberg, Tantoo Cardinal, Len Cariou, Marc Evan Jackson Original review date: October 11 (London Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: The painstaking stop-motion animation process applied to a tale on a scale rarely seen on this level is a visual knockout, and the story is a compelling one focused on a scrappy young heroine determined to fight back and save her baby brother after he is harrowingly abducted from the streets of Portland by a murder of crows. — PH RELATED: ‘Wildwood’ Review: Carey Mulligan Leads Voice Cast Of Laika’s Ambitious And Visually Stunning Stop-Motion Fantasy Epic – London Film Festival

‘A Talent For Murder’ Image Credit: Bleecker Street/LD Entertainment Release: Wide (October 23) Distributor: Bleecker Street Director: Anton Corbijn Writer: Joanna Murray-Smith Cast: Helen Mirren, Alden Ehrenreich, Olivia Cooke, Juliet Stevenson, James Faulkner Original review date: September 15 (Toronto Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: Helen Mirren, playing wildly against type, is a revelation in this flawed but very entertaining two-hander, which belongs in the unique subgenre of literary biographies in which a cult author’s life is investigated through the highly specific prism of their work. — DW RELATED: ‘A Talent For Murder’ Review: Helen Mirren Is Mesmerizing As Tortured Genius Crime Writer Patricia Highsmith – Toronto Film Festival

‘You Can See Everything’ Image Credit: A24 / Everett Collection Release: Wide (October 23) Distributor: A24 Directors: Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim Cast: Nathan Fielder, Elizabeth Holmes, Billy Evans, Christopher Abbott Original review date: September 7 (Telluride Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: The unusual (to say the least) documentary, which was shot in secrecy and runs nearly 3 hours, is unlike any I have ever seen in terms of pure access. Its title is appropriate: these people appear to hide nothing. — PH RELATED: ‘You Can See Everything’ Review: Shocking Elizabeth Holmes Documentary With Nathan Fielder Is Like No Other You Have Ever Seen – Telluride Film Festival

‘Love Language’ Image Credit: SXSW Release: Limited (October 23) Distributor: Vertical Director-screenwriter: Joey Power Cast: Chloë Grace Moretz, Anthony Ramos, Manny Jacinto, Isabel May, Lukas Gage, Billie Lourd, Chloe Fineman, Zach Zucker, Morgan Jay, Bobbi Althoff, Marchánt Davis, Dan Perrault Original review date: March 17 (SXSW) Deadline’s takeaway: Love Language is a return to classic rom-com form, with heart and humor, as well as a talented ensemble cast that beautifully brings Joey Power’s script to life against a dreamy Chicago backdrop. — GG RELATED: ‘Love Language’ Review: Chloë Grace Moretz Leads Messy Love Triangle While Capitalizing On Untapped Wedding Vows Market — SXSW

‘Possible Love’ Image Credit: Joo Jae-bum/Netflix Release: Limited (October 23) Distributor: Netflix Director: Lee Chang-dong Screenwriters: Lee Chang-dong and Oh Jung-Mi Cast: Jeon Do-Yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung, Cho Yeo-Jeung Original review date: September 6 (Venice Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: In some ways Lee Chang-dong‘s first film in eight years, which is South Korea’s official entry into the International Feature Film Oscar race , might remind you of the class divide in Bong Joon Ho’s Oscar-winning Parasite . But with a pandemic between that release and this one, Lee’s film carries a poignant subtext: a certain desire for love and longing in a world more split apart than ever, and one which for many seems like it all is out of reach. — PH RELATED: ‘Possible Love’ Review: Lee Chang -dong’s South Korean International Oscar Entry Is Powerful Story Of Class And Desire – Venice Film Festival

UPDATED with statements from Netflix and Lin after 8:44 a.m. post: Dan Lin is out as film boss at Netflix in a move that has been largely speculated for weeks. Insiders at the streamer have denied that Lin and even Bela Bajaria were on the chopping block, but here we are.

Lin is meeting with his feature staff Monday morning for a post-mortem after the news. Per sources close to the situation, a successor to Lin won’t be named until the arrival of Peter Rice, who is taking over Netflix’s Chief Content Officer role from Bajaria.

Netflix Names Peter Rice As Chief Content Officer

Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said this morning in a statement: “I started working with Dan well before he joined us in 2024 and his strength as a producer was always clear. Once he joined Netflix, I saw up close how his dedication to quality filmmaking, rigor around dealmaking and strategy, and collaborative spirit elevated our film business. I’m grateful to Dan for everything he’s done for Netflix films.”

Watch on Deadline

Lin added, “It’s been a great privilege to lead this incredible team and work with amazing filmmakers and talent to bring their movies to the world. Thank you to Ted, Greg and Bela for the opportunity.”

We caught up with Sarandos recently and asked whether more cuts were coming, following a week in which the streamer announced 1,000 layoffs , or 6% of its global workforce. In what seemed like a polite dodge, he winked and stepped away; interpret that as you may.

While this was going, we hear Lin was informed of his firing over the weekend.

Lin’s exit comes in the wake of last week’s pink-slips and Netflix’s recent slow growth, and minimal overall viewership spike. Wall Street is bracing for what is expected to be a downer quarter from the OTT service. At the time of this post, Netflix shares were trading at $69.76, off 1%; the 52-week high on Netflix stock is $124.86. A companywide town hall scheduled for Wednesday at Netflix with Sarandos and co-CEO Greg Peters will certainly be an interesting one.

RELATED: Netflix Shakeup: Peter Rice Is Welcomed Back To Executive Ranks While Bela Bajaria’s Exit Has Layoff-Weary Staff Bracing For More Upheaval

Many were shocked when the ax swung last week and it missed Lin’s head, landing on his lieutenant co-head of film Doug Belgrad . It was seen that Belgrad was an extra layer at the top of Netflix’s film brass that could easily be let go, dollar-wise. Lin was expected to be safe until Rice took over officially on October 26. It was at that point in time the exec planned to assess the situation.

What is all boils down to is this question: Netflix, what is it you exactly want? All of streaming has turned into basic cable as we get farther away from Covid, and Netflix looked to Lin in April 2024 post-Scott Stuber to ratchet down the quantity of features and at a lower cost. He arrived after being a producer at his own hub, Rideback. From 2008-2024, Lin produced movies that minted $6 billion at the global box office.

Lin did exactly what Netflix asked, steering away from overpriced $200 million-plus, non-downstream features like Red Notice, The Irishman and The Electric State .

However, he had a no-nonsense approach to filmmakers, and hand no problem reportedly pushing back on prestige content creators like Greta Gerwig and Ben Affleck. During the Lin regime, one source told us that relationships with filmmakers were fraying. Recently, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth filmmaker David Fincher opted not to renew his longtime exclusive contract with the streamer. That said, we’re also hearing there was never any bad blood between Fincher and Lin.

During Lin’s run, Netflix saw its most viewed movie of all-time, Sony’s KPop Demon Hunters (325.1M global views). However, that was greenlit under the Stuber administration. For Lin and Belgrad, their bragging rights include War Machine ($80M production cost, 147M views), the animated movie Swapped (144.9M views, which broke into the streamer’s top 10 all-time list), The Rip ($100M production cost, 136M views), Happy Gilmore 2 (135.1M), Apex (129M), Thrash (100M views) and People We Meet on Vacation ($14M production cost, 77.1M). Still there wasn’t a consistent reseeding of the Top 10 Most Popular list like there was during the Stuber era.

Also during the Lin regime, he acquired two-time Oscar winner Emila P é rez in addition to the streamer’s current awards contender, Cannes winner La Bola Negra.

Just as Lin is being shown the door, Netflix is finally embracing theatrical with respectable window releases and the reporting of grosses for select Q3, Q4 and Q1 titles including next year’s $200M+ Gerwig-directed Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew. In the four-theater New York City and Los Angeles launch of La Bola Negra this weekend, Netflix done good on a small scale as the pic notched the best opening per-screen average for a Spanish movie of $69,300, and the second best overall for a non-English movie after Parasite ‘s $13K.

If Netflix wants its movies to be a gong around the world, then it needs to embrace theatrical. That’s a tough maneuver for them since Wall Street doesn’t want them to be a traditional motion picture studio. In the streamer’s pursuit of Warner Bros, Sarandos began to drink the Kool-Aid on theatrical, conceding to a 45-day exclusive theatrical window (though to streaming, not PVOD; still not an ideal situation for exhibitors or filmmakers).

Now that Netflix is reporting grosses, will it spend for the weekend win? Before, the streamer would shove films into limited theaters to qualify for the Oscars, a strategy that doubled as an in-theater advertisement for the service. So far, Netflix’s No. 1 movie at the weekend box office was late August 2025’s KPop Demon Hunters Singalong with $19M.

It’s interesting to note that at a presser earlier this year, Bajaria and Lin were not in lockstep when asked about the streamer’s future with theatrical after losing the Warner Bros bid. Following Sarandos’ public campaign to guarantee an exclusive 45-day window, Bajaria took Netflix’s standard line about theatrical: It’s not what the company is about; it’s there for stunting purposes. Lin was more optimistic, saying, “Give us time.”

The Mike And Pam Of It All

After being passed over by Skydance for top jobs at the new post-merger Paramount-Warner Bros, we hear that former Warner Bros Motion Picture bosses Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy are in the home stretch this week of finalizing the payout of their WB contracts by David Ellison. Until they’re closed, they can’t entertain job offers.

Those close to De Luca tell us he’d have no problems reporting into Rice if offered the Netflix job, though Netflix would need to make a fire-breathing commitment to theatrical. The notion of a 45-day theatrical window to streaming isn’t a prospect De Luca (and Abdy) could make to the filmmakers with which they’ve worked, e.g., Ryan Coogler, Paul Thomas Anderson, Ridley Scott. One theory, that De Luca and Abdy are bound to raise capital for their own feature operation, seems like the more practical future for them.

All this smoke over De Luca and Abdy heading to Netflix came about due to a friendly lunch they had with Sarandos. The meet-up has spawned gossip that Sarandos was full-on courting the duo.

If Sarandos and Rice bring in the filmmaker-friendly duo, the question becomes whether they’ll put up guardrails around them. When it came to De Luca and Abdy justifying the lofty costs for Anderson’s One Battle After Another, Coogler’s Sinners, Tom Cruise’s Digger and so on, David Zaslav didn’t blink an eye. Will Sarandos allow them the same greenlight independence he granted Stuber? Or will he expect them to count coins like Lin? Riddle us that, Mr. Sarandos.

“Netflix isn’t a place where they talk about film,” says one creator who has worked with them. “They’re all about the process, the algorithm and breaking the code, which still makes Lin a good workhorse for them as he’s also about process.”

There’s a rumor out there that despite the notion that De Luca and Abdy are joined at the hip, historically they haven’t been. Some believe there’s a world in which Abdy could entertain an offer sans De Luca from Netflix once her WB contract is paid out. “Sure, there is a world where that could happen,” says one source with knowledge of the situation.

Still, there’s no solid definite word as to who might fill Lin’s vacancy. No interview process is going on as of yet.

A rival studio boss complimented over the weekend, “I think you’ll be surprised as to who Peter Rice selects.”

Meanwhile, we hear Lin will not be headed back to Rideback, the label he created, though he still has an interest in the company. Rideback and Netflix have a production deal.

But still, no matter how the greenlight process is improved at Netflix, there’s a new sign of the times for the streamer.

“If you want to know where the young crowd is looking, Meta just introduced Muse. People are heading back to cinemas, and streaming has become basic cable,” said one Netflix vet. “They can change [and] shuffle as many executives as they want, and it still won’t make a difference.”

article_text:
Curry apresentava saúde precária desde que sofreu um AVC em 2012.

O ator Tim Curry , conhecido por seu trabalho em filmes como “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” e “Esqueceram de Mim 2: Perdido em Nova York” e séries como “IT – A Coisa”, morreu na última terça-feira (25) aos 80 anos.

A perda foi confirmada pela amiga e empresária de Curry, Marcia Hurwitz, em declaração (via Deadline ):

“Ao longo de sua vida, ele se recusou a ser rotulado ou limitado pelas expectativas alheias. Durante cinco décadas, transitou com fluidez entre a comédia, o terror, o drama e a música, encantando a si mesmo e a sua legião de fãs com suas inúmeras e dinâmicas personas… Ele é, dependendo de a quem se pergunte, o Dr. Frank-N-Furter definitivo, o Pennywise definitivo, o homem que transformou o monólogo da cena de morte de um mordomo em ‘Detetive’ em um momento cômico memorável, ou simplesmente ‘aquela voz inesquecível’ de um desenho animado adorado da infância de alguém. “Poucos atores podem afirmar ter deixado tantas marcas distintas na cultura pop e, embora tenha sofrido um derrame debilitante em 2012, ele continuou a ampliar suas realizações como artista e, mais recentemente, como escritor. Apesar de ser amplamente conhecido por seus personagens inimitáveis ​​e extravagantes e por suas apresentações vibrantes, seus maiores legados para aqueles que o conheceram foram sua mente curiosa e expansiva e seu coração generoso e gentil — ambos mantendo-se abertos e cheios de expectativa até o seu último suspiro.”

Curry apresentava saúde precária desde que sofreu um acidente vascular cerebral grave em 2012. Ele utilizava cadeira de rodas desde o AVC e a cirurgia cerebral a que foi submetido na sequência.

Além dos filmes já citados, Curry também se destacou por seu trabalho no filme “Detetive”, baseado no clássico jogo de tabuleiro, “Annie”, “O Retorno da Família Addams” e “Todo Mundo em Pânico 2”, entre tantos outros. Ele também tinha um amplo catálogo como dublador, tendo dado voz a personagens como o Chanceler Palpatine na série de animação “Star Wars: The Clone Wars” e em desenhos como “Os Anjinhos”.

Tim Curry não deixa filhos ou parceiros, mas deixa um legado incomparável e duradouro.

article_text:
A former Philadelphia Museum of Art executive admitted on Friday to using company credit cards to make approximately $30,000 in personal purchases, the Inquirer reports .

Latasha Harling, the museum’s former chief people and diversity officer, pleaded guilty to receiving stolen property, averting a trial that had been scheduled for Friday.

Common Pleas Court Judge Leon King II sentenced Harling, 44, to five years of probation for the misdemeanor offense. King also ordered her to pay the museum $30,000 in restitution in monthly installments of at least $500, beginning in January. If she pays the full amount before her probation ends, however, Harling may request early termination of her probation.

Harling joined the museum in November 2023 as its inaugural chief people officer (CPO), overseeing human resources and diversity initiatives. Her budgetary responsibilities, the Inquirer noted, included access to corporate credit cards. An affidavit of probable cause filed in connection with her arrest recounts how museum officials grew suspicious of her activities in January 2025, after being alerted to a series of significant, seemingly personal purchases on her credit card statements. A subsequent audit by the museum’s chief financial officer found that Harling had charged $58,885 in personal expenses to the card since her hiring.

Harling was offered the opportunity to repay $32,565 to the museum, the affidavit states. She resigned shortly thereafter, with the credit card expenses still outstanding. The museum then sought to recover the money: The following February, Harling signed a promissory note agreeing to repay $19,380 over three months. After receiving no payments by April, the museum contacted police.

A spokesperson for the museum said in a statement that its officials are “grateful that the case” is resolved and that “we look forward to returning our focus to the exhibitions, programs, and experiences we provide for our community.”

article_text:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains minor spoilers for “ Whalefall ,” out now in theaters.

In the new feature “Whalefall,” Jay ( Austin Abrams ) is a grieving son searching for his father’s (Josh Brolin) remains off the coast of California. As he dives deeper, Jay encounters a giant squid being chased by an 80-foot, 60-ton sperm whale. When the goliaths of the ocean battle it out, Jay finds himself sucked into the whale just as the squid’s tentacles wrap around him, proving to be a force he can’t contend with. Jay finds himself in the belly of the whale with only an hour’s worth of oxygen left as he fights to find his way out.

Fremantle Takes Singapore Dating Format ‘Wingman’ Global in Mediacorp Deal

What follows is an intense, anxiety-driven and claustrophobic adventure, with Brolin’s voice and flashbacks guiding Jay along the way.

Popular on Variety

“It’s an intense experience, and that’s what we were going for,” says the film’s production designer Ramsey Avery.

Avery achieved that because he created practical whale sets, including a 30-foot whale head with a functional tongue mounted on an animatronic arm, allowing it to open and close. Filming in water and in camera using practical effects provided additional challenges, with the design of the set varying depending on where inside the whale Jay was located. The process began with extensive research.

Research

Avery started by examining autopsy photos of sperm whales and working closely with Dr. Joy Reidenberg, a biomedical research scientist. “She shared with me autopsies in the morning. I would get up at 6 a.m., look at autopsies with her as she was cutting open whales and explaining things to me.”

But that still didn’t give him a sense of what the inside of a whale’s stomach looked like when it was alive and in water.

“We found out very quickly that we don’t know very much. But we do have cameras going into the bellies of orcas, dolphins and porpoises, so we were able to start with that and see what they look like when they’re filled with fluids and when they’re moving.”

Building the Whale

Avery began with the key stomach set, which he calls “stomach number one.” This is where Jay spends most of his time. Director Brian Duffield wanted everything to be in water, so Avery built a 60-foot-wide tank that was 20 feet deep. “We ended up building about 30 feet of the whale’s head that we could put into the tank, and it had an articulating mouth and we could move it forward on a ram and back.”

He collaborated with the stunts team and rigging team, as well as the film’s cinematographer Aaron Morton, to understand what he needed. “We pushed as much of it being practically in-camera as we could,” says Avery. The tongue in the back of the whale’s throat was also a physical build, capable of moving up and down.

Finding the right material to construct the stomach was a challenge and required exploration. “It’s upholstery foam,” Avery reveals. “It’s two to three inches depending on where it is.”

The interior was made of multiple layers of translucent, colored silicone to create a viscous look. The exterior was covered with heavy-duty canvas and coated with glue for added rigidity, while still allowing flexibility. “This made the stomach look alive,” Avery explains.

The finished product required some additional digital effects work with Weta Workshop, but ultimately was “strong enough that it stood up for Jay being in it with water and stunt guys and camera and visual and special effects for six weeks.” Avery reveals the claustrophobia feeling comes from the inside. “The inside of the stomach is about eight feet wide and six feet tall when fully expanded,” Avery says. “Most of the time, though, it’s the size of a sleeping bag. It’s tight — just enough room for Jay and one or two cameras.”

Rigs and Movement

To simulate the motion of the whale, Avery experimented with different techniques. At first, he thought of using pistons on the outside or using ropes. But when they needed the whale to rise or dive, it couldn’t be done. “We had four different stomachs on different rigs to make that happen,” Avery says. “Our main stomach was on a small rig that always kept the whale in motion and swimming.” And there was a spinning rig that was like a washing machine for when the whale would spin.

Stomach Bile

In one sequence of the film, Jay finds himself in the whale’s stomach bile. All the colors depicted inside the whale were based on real-life anatomy. “The back of the throat is white, and the first stomach — the chewing stomach — is muscular and white with some pink tones,” Avery explains. “The second stomach, with its red acids, is pink.” These colors also mirrored Jay’s emotional journey. “He’s going from something that feels somewhat OK to ‘I don’t want to be here. This is a horrible place to be.’”

Creating the stomach’s viscous bile was another challenge. “Brian [Duffield] wanted it to feel like a slog for Jay to move through, like he really had to work,” Avery says. To achieve this, the team used methyl cellulose (a thickening agent) mixed with various additives to create a texture similar to oatmeal. They also manufactured silicone bits and pieces to simulate floating debris in the water and added bubble ports to mimic the effect of acid eating away at objects.

Avery explains, “All of this was placed on a large teeter-totter rig. That allowed us to create big, sloshing movements to make it look like the whale was diving and the stomach acids were churning around Jay.”

article_text:
Editor’s Note: This review was originally published at SXSW 2026. World of Wonder releases “ Manhood ” in select theaters starting Wednesday, October 28.

What if you could up your penis size a notch or two with a few spritzes of a needle? OK, it’s not that simple, but the PhaloFILL procedure highlighted by filmmaker Daniel Lombroso in his latest documentary, “ Manhood ,” aims to make penile enlargement procedures about as easy (and commonplace) as Botox.

Dallas entrepreneur Bill Moore, who is quite proudly Botoxed and fillered-up himself, patented the minimally invasive procedure (don’t call it plastic surgery!), promising to make insecure men feel whole again. Or at least a bit thicker, anyway. Lombroso’s skillfully constructed film is funny in the best and worst ways: funny because it’s in on the joke but “funny” because of how the majority of the audience might feel embarrassed just by watching it. The director understands the humor inherent to this situation, but he also understands the sad parts, the well of male insecurity it’s all coming from — locating that especially in an OnlyFans camboy who comes to Moore after a catastrophic procedure at a rival clinic has left him with a dick full of nodules.

Penis size is a major psychic hang-up for men across both the straight and gay communities; as a gay man, I can attest to these particular pressures within a community where both partners have penises, and a community that already primatizes physical attributes over the inner self. Moore’s practice, as “Manhood” illustrates, has turned small genitalia (or even those not especially small, even though the body-dysmorphic men they’re attached to insist they are because of society, etc., etc.) into a growing business while seeking to universalize the dick-size complex. “Every man wants a bigger penis,” the bio-hacking mogul says at one point. Do they? Using hyaluronic acid — which is the same stuff I put on my face every morning — he’s ready to give you the big penis of your dreams, and an even bigger bill.

One of Moore’s clients, endearingly self-defeating Arizona-resident Ruben, is a father of five who is under serious financial strain due to gambling addiction and also perhaps a penile enhancement addiction. He’s a repeat customer of Moore’s, having spent tens of thousands on multiple procedures that — this is important — have not increased the length of his penis but certainly the girth several sizes over. Penis lengthening is not something any doctor wishing to avoid malpractice has successfully figured out, despite grotesque procedures in ancient times, from mechanical lengthening to snake bites, that purported to do so.

Meanwhile, though Ruben’s wife was plenty happy with his God-given girth, her husband (who has children with multiple women) keeps going back to Dr. Moore for yet another below-the-belt tune-up. “Manhood” is loud and clear in its uncensored depiction of these injections into men’s members as they drop their drawers and splay prostrate on the operating table. Don’t forget the gasp-inducing images of dicks mangled by one Dr. Loria in New York City, who has proudly refused malpractice insurance but allegedly left a number of men deformed after pumping them up with chunky-looking filler. Lombroso applies the same close-up care as he did in his 2022 documentary “White Noise,” unflinchingly gazing into the rise of the alt-right movement and neo-Nazis in America. “Manhood” isn’t reinventing the form — even as the men it follows are reinventing theirs — but it’s super charming in its straightforward aims at tackling taboo material.

Contrasting Ruben’s heterosexual working-class charm, meek-mannered David Smith, a former OnlyFans camboy turned Florida nursing student, is one such emotional and physical casualty of Dr. Loria’s alleged malpractice. (Loria, by the way, is an unapologetic talking head in this documentary, too.) Already coming from a devoutly conservative family that rejected his homosexuality, the tight-bodied, petite David felt insecure about his dick size while becoming a fast-rising star on OnlyFans. He’s been left with what Dr. Moore describes as “the penis of an alien.” Moore not only offers David the promise to fix his penis, he also invites him into his bed to be the apparent third in Moore’s relationship with his partner. The three are seen sharing a hotel bed while traveling to see a specialist who will need to perform drastic surgery on David’s member, and it’s not clear what Lambroso, or his camera, thinks of this arrangement, which is why this decidedly non-invasive, nonjudgmental documentary works so well.

“I can fill your penis with filler, but I cannot fill the hole in your heart,” Moore tells his patient/lover David. The patient-doctor relationship here is certainly ethically questionable, but at what point are ethics just sort of tossed out the window when we’re talking dicks? Still, Lombroso takes his subject and his subjects seriously, and treats them with respect. David, marveling near-tears at the results of his reconstructive surgery, makes for a moving moment — who knew a documentary about penile enhancement could touch a nerve and the heart, too?

Grade: B+

“Manhood” premiered at SXSW 2026. The film opens in select theaters starting Wednesday, October 28.
excerpt_original: Daniel Lombroso's certainly bizarre but sensitive portrait follows a PhalloFill entrepreneur (it's what it sounds like) and two of his clients as they walk us through a cosmetic phenomenon whose main clientele are insecure men.

article_text:
Einen rund 2000 Jahre alten Marmor-Torso eines römischen Kaisers ins Wohnzimmer stellen? Das kann ein anonymer Bieter jetzt machen. Dafür hat er rund 34 Millionen Dollar bezahlt – und lange gekämpft

Ein rund 2000 Jahre alter Marmor-Torso eines römischen Kaisers ist in New York für den Rekordpreis von 34,3 Millionen Dollar versteigert worden. Das sei rund dreimal so viel wie vorab geschätzt und der höchste Preis, der je bei einer Auktion für eine römische Antiquität erzielt worden sei, teilte das Auktionshaus Sotheby's mit.

Fünf Bieter hätten sich dafür fast eine Viertelstunde lang einen Wettstreit geliefert. Wer am Ende den Zuschlag bekam, teilte das Auktionshaus zunächst nicht mit. Der Torso sei in sehr gutem Zustand und stelle einen Kaiser aus der Julisch-Claudischen Dynastie im antiken Rom dar.

title_original: 那些在陽剛影史中遊蕩的女子──《里昂的跫音》、《煙硝下的斑斕》、《野草蔓生》
title_zh: 那些在陽剛影史中遊蕩的女子──《里昂的跫音》、《煙硝下的斑斕》、《野草蔓生》
summary_zh: 来源摘录：唯有以感同身受為前提，遊蕩才不只是遊蕩，也不只是敘事結構，而是女性在不同處境中，因其性別而面臨各種無可避免的困難時，對生存與前路的摸索。《煙硝下的斑斕》的薩瑪，也許比原先過著安舒的婚家生活的柯姿（《野草蔓生》）、伊莉莎白（《里昂的跫音》），更能展現「困難」為何是女性／性別化的。 這篇文章 那些在陽剛影史中遊蕩的女子──《里昂的跫音》、《煙硝下的斑斕》、《野草蔓生》 最早出現於 釀電影 。

4 項獨立精神獎提名，可謂一鳴驚人。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "萊卡特本人對空窗期的解釋，與上述訪談同樣直截了當： 「自九〇年代中期起，我整整十年都拍不成電影。很大程度是因為我是個女人。這絕對是募資困難的一大原因，那期間根本無法推動任何計畫，所以我索性撂下一句『去你的』，便改拍 Super8mm 去了。」 此時的她剛拍完第 4 部劇情長片《米克的近路》（Meek’s Cutoff，2010），與《野草蔓生》同樣具有從女性視角顛覆陽剛電影傳統（公路／西部）的企圖；只是截至當時，她仍須依賴在巴德學院（Brad College）任教的收入，才能繼續拍電影。（註 2）"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "​萊卡特認同柯姿，但柯姿不完全是萊卡特，而儘管《野草蔓生》在萊卡特出生、成長的邁阿密取景，也不完全是她的自傳；但藉由結合創作者的個人經歷，及其所反映的業內情況為閱讀策略，柯姿的遊蕩與萊卡特在女性電影之路上的跌跌撞撞，仍能相互為喻。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "而如果說，《野草蔓生》呈現的「女性遊蕩」雖似無中生有、漫無目的，在戲外卻有實質的呼應對象，那麼《里昂的跫音》中的女性遊蕩，亦同樣呼應現實──致力於為工人爭取權利的法國女性主義先驅，芙蘿拉．特里斯坦（Flora Tristan，1803－1844）。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://img.vocus.cc/B17owtS9gNvnwc_7La6jSPr9iRRDiFJv_KGolWKJLLs/w:740/f:jpg/plain/https://images.vocus.cc/0aa018db-33cc-4434-9c1c-2ce75b310097.jpg", "alt": "《里昂的跫音》電影劇照／劇照提供：台灣國際女性影展", "caption": "", "credit": "釀電影"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《里昂的跫音》電影劇照／劇照提供：台灣國際女性影展"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "​乍看之下，《里昂的跫音》除了同樣由女主角的遊蕩引導敘事，與《野草蔓生》之間似乎再無可比之處。再者，隨著敘事推進，柯姿的遊蕩是漸趨清晰的，她在結局中確確實實地殺了人，其遊蕩亦因而成為貨真價實的逃亡；相反，《里昂的跫音》的伊莉莎白（Elizabeth）是「出師有名」，她到里昂追蹤特里斯坦的足跡，但採用有別於傳統歷史研究的方法論，也使此行彷彿一場無果的遊蕩。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "值得注意的是，正是在這點上，《里昂的跫音》挑戰的不只是必須抽離自我、以求客觀地檢視史料的研究傳統，還有必須有始有終的傳統敘事。伊莉莎白的研究方法，是根據特里斯坦的日記，親自走訪她留下足跡之處。 事實上，她正是被這本日記所迷住，遂拋下丈夫與幼女來到里昂，據她在電影開場自述，丈夫對她的決定頗不以為然。直到電影結束前，她致電丈夫，已聯絡不上他和女兒。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "假如《里昂的跫音》是一部「客觀地」記錄歷史事件的電影，那這些關於為人妻子及母親的「瑣事」，想必會被裁掉。 然而，當歷史學者問及伊莉莎白，為何錄下特里斯坦「可能聽過的腳步聲」，還有她「究竟在找什麼」時，伊莉莎白是這麼說的："}, {"type": "quote", "text": "「我試著想像她可能聽過的、可能看過的、可能聞過的色彩、聲響等等。在里昂這座她曾旅居一段時間的城市，我在重拾她當年的旅程。光是在圖書館和檔案庫做研究，光只是讀書沒辦法滿足我。要像這樣把自己放回另一個時代，是很吃力不討好的事⋯⋯我很清楚，我知道我不是她。我們要透過什麼才能記憶？當然是透過檔案，透過歷史人物來記憶。歷史學家要做的事，就是將自己隱藏在研究對象背後，讓他們自己說話，還原他們的生活，盡可能退居幕後。我們便是這樣，試圖甚至成功考掘出古人的生與死、生活方式、飲食習慣和情感生活。我在想，透過認同過往女性的痛楚、苦難和感受，我們能否將這些感受化為行動？而不是流於被動的理解。」（註 "《釀電影》編輯室以「女人沒有鄉愁」為策展專題，延伸「流動」一詞作為觀看當代世界的方法，循著穿行於城市與鄉野、家庭與個體、戰爭與和平之間的選擇，即從無法無家、無法有家，又何處不是家的概念出發，嘗試看見女性在巨大歷史的移動軌跡之中，曾經被隱匿、邊緣的流離。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "當「鄉愁」經常性地被放置在傳統父權結構底下，指涉國族敘事框架、血緣根源、既定秩序的眷戀與歸返，自破除疆界而起的遊牧，便關乎於女性電影中的身分、身體、時間與抗爭之路徑。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本次專題委邀策展人陳慧穎進行訪問，自「屬於她的遊蕩」單元的六部電影作品展開，重新爬梳半世紀的世界之變，與存於其中的不變；同時亦邀請獨立評論人陳穎，深入分析「屬於她的遊蕩」單元中，三部來自八〇、九〇年代的導演首作，以「移動」與「身體性」為軸，試論空間為性別運動、女性主義所開創的嶄新變革。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "圍繞著「跨越」、「移動」的概念，今年的「焦點影人」單元為非裔法國電影導演莎拉・馬羅多羅（Sarah Maldoror，1929－2020），本次也將收錄獨立評論人黃曦，自多部經典電影爬梳女性主義與反殖民運動、去殖民途徑的抵抗力量。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "延續關於時間、時代之思索，本專題另有三篇獨立評論，分別由獨立評論人許騰云、小說家趙鴻祐與新銳評論人黎思行執筆。透過普拉迪・克里申（Pradip Krishen）《安尼閣來舞這齣》（In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones，1989）回到七〇年代，與作家阿蘭達蒂・洛伊（Arundhati Roy）進行跨越世代對話；接著隨克萊兒・西蒙（Claire Simon）《我們的青春與安妮艾諾》（Writing Life – Annie Ernaux Through the Eyes of High School Students，2025）與當代學子的對讀，將書寫轉化為面向未來、身分的路徑；最後由琳恩・薩克斯（Lynne Sachs）《相遇皆有痕》（Every Contact Leaves a Trace，2025）的實驗性展開評析，記述散文電影無有時間，卻凝刻空間、記憶的痕跡。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最後，本專題亦與《沒有的派對》（Sometimes, I Imagine Them All at a Party，2026）導演丹妮亞拉・麥蘭妮・胡勒（Daniela Melanie Goode）展開深入對談，自導演十餘年後執起攝影機，透過多重影像媒介將創傷記憶轉化為與公共對話，甚至對抗體制的政治力量，以期提出一種嶄新的、當代的對話空間是──「女人沒有鄉愁」的起點不在故土，而在踏出疆界、凝視創傷、重構語言與時間的游蕩中，我們如何在生命的蜿蜒之中，持續闖蕩？"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "✹「女人沒有鄉愁」專題閱讀情由此 ✹", article_text:
撰文／陳穎 劇照提供／台灣國際女性影展 責任編輯／黃曦 核稿編輯／黃曦

猶記得 2018 年的第 25 屆台灣國際女性影展（下稱女影），是以安妮．華達（Agnès Varda，1928－2019）的 《無法無家》（Vagabond，1985） 揭開序幕的。甫開演，但見女子陳屍在鄉間村落旁的田溝。 已逝的她無法自陳，我們只能從陌生人對她的描述，拼湊出她生前的最後足跡──四處遊蕩。這些陌生人，是她在遊蕩期間的一面之緣，遂無意見證了女子人生的最後階段。但透過第三方的陳述，我們頂多推敲，而無法證實她是誰，又為何遊蕩。

「遊蕩」在女性文本中，具有專屬於女性的意義。《無法無家》固然是奠定此道的經典之作之一，而在該片被修復並作為女影開幕片的 8 年後，2026 年的 第 33 屆台灣國際女性影展 ，端出了 「屬於她的遊蕩」 單元。

要談「女性遊蕩」，固然不一定要從華達說起。組成此單元的六部作品，就有兩部分別早於《無法無家》或與之同期──德國導演克勞迪亞．馮阿萊曼（Claudia von Alemann）的《里昂的跫音》（Blind Spot，1981）和黎巴嫩導演喬瑟琳．薩博（Jocelyne Saab）的《煙硝下的斑斕》（The Razor’s Edge，1985）。

此二作再加上美國導演凱莉．萊卡特（Kelly Reichardt）的《野草蔓生》（River of Grass，1994），與單元中另外三部近作──《夏娜衝衝衝》（Shana，2026）、《風口》（Wind Gap，2025）、《木蘭何處》（Where Comes Mulan，2026）──亦形成可對讀的古今對照。

《野草蔓生》電影劇照／劇照提供：台灣國際女性影展

本文將集中討論上述三部相對而言的「老電影」，嘗試在以三者（及《無法無家》）面世於相若時期為基礎，追溯早期女性導演對「遊蕩」這一元素的運用，從而探討「遊蕩」在女性主義電影傳統中的特殊意義──亦即，遊蕩為何是女性主義的影像實踐？

嚴格來說，此三作皆非此道之開端，但在《末路狂花》（Thelma & Louise，1991）致使此一傳統較為人知悉以前，它們起了承先啟後的作用； 同時，在「遊蕩」作為女性追尋某理想的象徵，並作為追蹤女性經歷的敘事路徑的兩大前提下，這些女性影像創作先驅，亦不受此限地探索、展現姑且稱為「女性遊蕩電影」的多樣性與可能性。

必須補充，《野草蔓生》其實晚於《末路狂花》，但作為後來者，反而可連同前作，視為對美式公路電影之陽剛傾向的擾動。然而，相對於在《末路狂花》前已拍下《異型》（Alien，1979）、 《銀翼殺手》（Blade Runner，1982） 的雷利．史考特（Ridley Scott），既是新人又是女性的萊卡特則無處不碰壁。

與萊卡特關係密切的美國新酷兒電影運動代表人物陶德．海恩斯（Todd Haynes），曾在訪問萊卡特時形容，無論在財務、物流與情感上，《野草蔓生》都是「夢魘等級的難拍」（a nightmare to get made），而她直認不諱，並以自身拍片困境為基礎，將自己比作女主角柯姿（Kurtz）：

「我完全認同她。我們都在嘗試摸索自己的路。我寫好了劇本，與它朝夕相處，也籌得資金，但還是得每天在拍攝現場，捍衛自己身為導演的地位。這還是我這輩子第一次覺得：『噢，我懂了，發生這些鳥事全因我是女人。』電影中的每個鏡頭，都是我奮力爭取而來，這實在有夠磨人，也是我所始料未及的。原本的結局並不長這樣，如今這樣結束，完全是我在拍攝過程中的經歷所致。柯姿演繹了我的幻想，正是這幻想使她得以越過各種鳥事，抵達彼端──只是我和她都發現，彼端只有更多鳥事。」 （註 1）

柯姿並非導演或影像工作者，而是被婚姻、育兒悶得發慌，繼而離家的小鎮主婦。她的離家既非由具體的事件觸發，更無確切的目的地。這樣的遊蕩狀態促成了她與魯蛇男的相遇，兩人糊裡糊塗地相遇，又糊裡糊塗地以為自己殺了人，隨即自我代入為「亡命鴛鴦」，並展開「逃亡之旅」。 一切都糊裡糊塗的，看起來根本稱不上「困局」，但萊卡特的這番經驗談，為電影提供了劇情以外的另一脈絡──陽剛電影工業中的女性處境。

《里昂的跫音》電影劇照／劇照提供：台灣國際女性影展

​完成《野草蔓生》這部「處女作」後，直到 2006 年，萊卡特才等到再拍劇情長片的機會。這段空窗期顯然與《野草蔓生》的品質無關，畢竟它分別入選柏林國際影展與日舞影展，並獲得 4 項獨立精神獎提名，可謂一鳴驚人。

萊卡特本人對空窗期的解釋，與上述訪談同樣直截了當： 「自九〇年代中期起，我整整十年都拍不成電影。很大程度是因為我是個女人。這絕對是募資困難的一大原因，那期間根本無法推動任何計畫，所以我索性撂下一句『去你的』，便改拍 Super8mm 去了。」 此時的她剛拍完第 4 部劇情長片《米克的近路》（Meek’s Cutoff，2010），與《野草蔓生》同樣具有從女性視角顛覆陽剛電影傳統（公路／西部）的企圖；只是截至當時，她仍須依賴在巴德學院（Brad College）任教的收入，才能繼續拍電影。（註 2）

​萊卡特認同柯姿，但柯姿不完全是萊卡特，而儘管《野草蔓生》在萊卡特出生、成長的邁阿密取景，也不完全是她的自傳；但藉由結合創作者的個人經歷，及其所反映的業內情況為閱讀策略，柯姿的遊蕩與萊卡特在女性電影之路上的跌跌撞撞，仍能相互為喻。

而如果說，《野草蔓生》呈現的「女性遊蕩」雖似無中生有、漫無目的，在戲外卻有實質的呼應對象，那麼《里昂的跫音》中的女性遊蕩，亦同樣呼應現實──致力於為工人爭取權利的法國女性主義先驅，芙蘿拉．特里斯坦（Flora Tristan，1803－1844）。

《里昂的跫音》電影劇照／劇照提供：台灣國際女性影展

​乍看之下，《里昂的跫音》除了同樣由女主角的遊蕩引導敘事，與《野草蔓生》之間似乎再無可比之處。再者，隨著敘事推進，柯姿的遊蕩是漸趨清晰的，她在結局中確確實實地殺了人，其遊蕩亦因而成為貨真價實的逃亡；相反，《里昂的跫音》的伊莉莎白（Elizabeth）是「出師有名」，她到里昂追蹤特里斯坦的足跡，但採用有別於傳統歷史研究的方法論，也使此行彷彿一場無果的遊蕩。

值得注意的是，正是在這點上，《里昂的跫音》挑戰的不只是必須抽離自我、以求客觀地檢視史料的研究傳統，還有必須有始有終的傳統敘事。伊莉莎白的研究方法，是根據特里斯坦的日記，親自走訪她留下足跡之處。 事實上，她正是被這本日記所迷住，遂拋下丈夫與幼女來到里昂，據她在電影開場自述，丈夫對她的決定頗不以為然。直到電影結束前，她致電丈夫，已聯絡不上他和女兒。

假如《里昂的跫音》是一部「客觀地」記錄歷史事件的電影，那這些關於為人妻子及母親的「瑣事」，想必會被裁掉。 然而，當歷史學者問及伊莉莎白，為何錄下特里斯坦「可能聽過的腳步聲」，還有她「究竟在找什麼」時，伊莉莎白是這麼說的：

「我試著想像她可能聽過的、可能看過的、可能聞過的色彩、聲響等等。在里昂這座她曾旅居一段時間的城市，我在重拾她當年的旅程。光是在圖書館和檔案庫做研究，光只是讀書沒辦法滿足我。要像這樣把自己放回另一個時代，是很吃力不討好的事⋯⋯我很清楚，我知道我不是她。我們要透過什麼才能記憶？當然是透過檔案，透過歷史人物來記憶。歷史學家要做的事，就是將自己隱藏在研究對象背後，讓他們自己說話，還原他們的生活，盡可能退居幕後。我們便是這樣，試圖甚至成功考掘出古人的生與死、生活方式、飲食習慣和情感生活。我在想，透過認同過往女性的痛楚、苦難和感受，我們能否將這些感受化為行動？而不是流於被動的理解。」（註 3）

《里昂的跫音》電影劇照／劇照提供：台灣國際女性影展

《煙硝下的斑斕》電影劇照／劇照提供：台灣國際女性影展

導演馮阿萊曼藉伊莉莎白之口所談的，不只是歷史研究的另類方法論，也是觀影的另一種方法。 這一觀影方法置身同感受於敘事邏輯之先，以這種方法觀看「女性遊蕩」，即不問其因果，而將重點放在「認同」與「同理」遊蕩女子及其經歷上。

唯有以感同身受為前提，遊蕩才不只是遊蕩，也不只是敘事結構，而是女性在不同處境中，因其性別而面臨各種無可避免的困難時，對生存與前路的摸索。 《煙硝下的斑斕》的薩瑪（Sama），也許比原先過著安舒的婚家生活的柯姿（音譯自 Cozy，如此命名顯然旨在反諷）、伊莉莎白，更能展現「困難」為何是女性／性別化的。

記者出身的薩博，在黎巴嫩內戰期間拍下此作，雖然是她的首部劇情長片，卻同時側記戰爭實況，也呼應她此前為飽受戰火摧殘的家鄉所拍，以「貝魯特三部曲」為代表作的一系列紀錄片。然而，當我們跟隨薩瑪在頹垣敗瓦中遊蕩，也將意外地發現，這位謎一般的靈動少女並不畏戰，更不受其束縛。

戰亂使本就處於弱勢的伊斯蘭婦女，承受更大的暴力與道德規訓──例如，其母強迫她接受「處女膜」修復手術──薩瑪卻在光天化日下高呼要當蕩婦，並沒來由地迷戀與之為鄰的中年畫家。

《煙硝下的斑斕》電影劇照／劇照提供：台灣國際女性影展

​我發現自己不太想同理薩瑪與這位⋯⋯似乎正被戰爭蠶食信念，並經歷中年危機的男子的忘年之戀，但薩瑪若即若離的遊蕩本身，也正質疑著目的導向的線性敘事，此目的包括：成全愛情。 然而，愛情當真是薩瑪的心之所屬嗎？

柯姿的犯罪、伊莉莎白的研究、薩瑪的愛情──也許我們只能，也只需要陪她們遊蕩一番，而不問「究竟在找什麼」。

《煙硝下的斑斕》電影劇照／劇照提供：台灣國際女性影展

註 2. 詳見《衛報》專訪 ，（The Guardian，2011.04.09）。其標題亦如萊卡特口吻般直截了當：「我如何為了拍攝《米克的近路》而徒步穿越俄勒岡州，然後重返教職」（“ how I trekked across Oregon for Meek’s Cutoff then returned to teaching ”）

《釀電影》女人沒有鄉愁──𝟤𝟢𝟤𝟨 台灣國際女性影展專題／圖像提供：釀電影

將於 2026 年 10 月 16 日正式開展的第 33 屆女性影展，以「非分擾動 Into the Drift」為年度視覺，藉由流動、穿梭的視覺意象，向當代持續變動的疆界、關係發出提問，嘗試在一個世紀的電影裡，尋找錨定自身位置，重新想像自由的樣貌。

《釀電影》編輯室以「女人沒有鄉愁」為策展專題，延伸「流動」一詞作為觀看當代世界的方法，循著穿行於城市與鄉野、家庭與個體、戰爭與和平之間的選擇，即從無法無家、無法有家，又何處不是家的概念出發，嘗試看見女性在巨大歷史的移動軌跡之中，曾經被隱匿、邊緣的流離。

當「鄉愁」經常性地被放置在傳統父權結構底下，指涉國族敘事框架、血緣根源、既定秩序的眷戀與歸返，自破除疆界而起的遊牧，便關乎於女性電影中的身分、身體、時間與抗爭之路徑。

本次專題委邀策展人陳慧穎進行訪問，自「屬於她的遊蕩」單元的六部電影作品展開，重新爬梳半世紀的世界之變，與存於其中的不變；同時亦邀請獨立評論人陳穎，深入分析「屬於她的遊蕩」單元中，三部來自八〇、九〇年代的導演首作，以「移動」與「身體性」為軸，試論空間為性別運動、女性主義所開創的嶄新變革。

圍繞著「跨越」、「移動」的概念，今年的「焦點影人」單元為非裔法國電影導演莎拉・馬羅多羅（Sarah Maldoror，1929－2020），本次也將收錄獨立評論人黃曦，自多部經典電影爬梳女性主義與反殖民運動、去殖民途徑的抵抗力量。

延續關於時間、時代之思索，本專題另有三篇獨立評論，分別由獨立評論人許騰云、小說家趙鴻祐與新銳評論人黎思行執筆。透過普拉迪・克里申（Pradip Krishen）《安尼閣來舞這齣》（In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones，1989）回到七〇年代，與作家阿蘭達蒂・洛伊（Arundhati Roy）進行跨越世代對話；接著隨克萊兒・西蒙（Claire Simon）《我們的青春與安妮艾諾》（Writing Life – Annie Ernaux Through the Eyes of High School Students，2025）與當代學子的對讀，將書寫轉化為面向未來、身分的路徑；最後由琳恩・薩克斯（Lynne Sachs）《相遇皆有痕》（Every Contact Leaves a Trace，2025）的實驗性展開評析，記述散文電影無有時間，卻凝刻空間、記憶的痕跡。

最後，本專題亦與《沒有的派對》（Sometimes, I Imagine Them All at a Party，2026）導演丹妮亞拉・麥蘭妮・胡勒（Daniela Melanie Goode）展開深入對談，自導演十餘年後執起攝影機，透過多重影像媒介將創傷記憶轉化為與公共對話，甚至對抗體制的政治力量，以期提出一種嶄新的、當代的對話空間是──「女人沒有鄉愁」的起點不在故土，而在踏出疆界、凝視創傷、重構語言與時間的游蕩中，我們如何在生命的蜿蜒之中，持續闖蕩？

article_text:
Jess Gabor and Arthur Langlie will star in “He Talks to Me,” a psychological thriller from director Christina Kallas and screenwriter Alejandro Adams, Variety can reveal exclusively.

Mike S. Ryan developed the project and will produce through his banner Greyshack Films. Derrick Tseng will also produce.

According to an official logline, “He Talks to Me” follows “Melody (Gabor), a young single mother in rural Arkansas, who is followed home by local police officer Bryce Hagan (Langlie) for what begins as a casual interrogation and spirals into a harrowing test of survival, coercion and endurance.” Other cast members include Sayra Player, Adam David Thompson and Ryan Siegel.

Related Stories

‘Musk’ TikTok Ad Account Temporarily Suspended Ahead of Documentary's Wide Release

‘Musk’ Director Alex Gibney Confirms Universal Wavered in Planning Overseas Release, Says He Tried to Interview Elon Musk: ‘His Response Was Writing “Gibney Is a Douche”’

Other projects from Kallas, a two-time Berlinale and Slamdance alumna, include “Paris is in Harlem” and “The Rainbow Experiment.” She is a former president of the Federation of Screenwriters in Europe and a member of the Actors Studio.

Gabor recently wrapped production on Tony Goldwyn ‘s “Hello Darkness” and can next be seen in a recurring role in Season 3 of “ Daredevil: Born Again .” Her other recent film credits include David Michod’s “Christy,” “The Friend” with Bill Murray and Greyson Horst’s “Throuple.” On the small screen, she starred in Season 2 of the Paramount+ series “School Spirits” and had a breakout performance on Season 9 and Season 10 of “Shameless.”

Arthur was last seen in Kent Jones’ 2025 drama “Late Fame,” which starred Willem Dafoe and Greta Lee. His upcoming credits include “Cut Your Teeth,” from director Samuel Goodwin and producer Aaron Moorhead, and” Trash Pandas,” from director Ana Brown and producer Peter Cambor.

Gabor is repped by Anonymous Content, Buchwald, and Jackoway Austen Tyerman; Langlie by UTA; Adams by Range Media Partners; Thompson by CGF Talent; Player by Exclusive Artists Agency; and Siegel by Avenue B Talent.

article_text:
写真家・伊丹豪の個展「a plan for all things」が、2026年10月3日から27日まで、東京・神楽坂のCAVE-AYUMI GALLERYで開催される。本展では、すべて自身の自宅で撮影した新作を発表。会場デザインを建築家の板坂留五が手がける。

伊丹はこれまで、画面内のすべてにピントを合わせる「全焦点」の写真を通して、写真を「見ること」と「撮ること」の関係を考察してきた。被写体の一つだけを際立たせるのではなく、画面に存在するものを等しく鮮明に写すことで、鑑賞者の視線に無意識のうちに生まれるヒエラルキーを揺さぶる。一方、その写真は鮮やかな色彩や大胆な構図にも特徴があり、鑑賞者は視覚的な面白さに引き込まれながら、次第に「何が意図され、何が偶然なのか」という問いへと導かれていく。

今回、伊丹が被写体とするのは、自宅にある家具や日用品など、ごく身近なものだ。それらを選び、動かし、配置することで画面を構成していく。その背景には、過去に見てきた写真や絵画、美術の構造を、生活空間に存在する物の配置へと置き換える行為がある。撮影を終えれば配置は解体され、実際の空間から消えてしまう。写真の中にだけ、そこに存在した物と、すでに存在しない一時的な関係性が残される。

展覧会タイトルの「a plan for all things」には、「plan＝計画」と「plane＝平面」という二つの意味が重ねられている。物を選び、配置して撮影するという「計画」と、それらすべてが同じ密度で定着される写真という「平面」。美術からの引用も日用品も、作為も偶然も、一枚の表面では等価な存在として並ぶ。

「写真は目の前を複製することしか出来ない」と伊丹は語る。だからこそ、何を写し、どのように配置し、どの技術によって複製するのか。その選択の積み重ねに、写真を撮る行為の誠実さを見いだしている。作品の中で何が重要なのか、何が偶然なのかという答えはあえて明示されない。判断は見る側へと委ねられ、「何を見るか」という行為そのものが、私たち自身の価値判断を浮かび上がらせていく。

さらに本展では、これまでも建築家やデザイナーらとの協働を行ってきた伊丹の姿勢を引き継ぎ、板坂留五が展示空間を設計する。板坂は新たな造形を加えるのではなく、「しんとした空気の部屋」をつくり、鑑賞者が写真へゆっくりと近づいていける空間を構想。ギャラリーにもともと存在する壁や床、躯体の凹凸と伊丹の写真を組み合わせることで、写真に表れる独特の物の捉え方を空間へと拡張する。

タイトル

伊丹豪「a plan for all things」

場所

CAVE-AYUMI GALLERY（東京都新宿区矢来町114 高橋ビルB2）

会期

2026年10月3日（土）〜27日（火）

時間

12:00〜19:00

休み

水・木曜日

料金

無料

URL

https://www.nest-a.tokyo

translated_excerpt_zh: 摄影师伊丹刚个展《万事万物的计划》将于2026年10月3日至27日在东京神乐坂CAVE-AYUMI GALLERY举办。本次展览中，他将展出新作品，全部是在自己家中拍摄的。建筑师板坂鲁吾 (Rugo Itasaka) 设计了场馆。

title_original: Commonality and Differences: Kenji Ishizaka on Asian Future at the Tokyo International Film Festival
editorial_title_zh: 共性与差异：东京国际电影节上的石坂健治谈“亚洲未来”单元
editorial_excerpt_zh: 越是仔细审视国际电影真实、有形的世界，人们就越会意识到自己对正在发生的事情其实并没有连贯的概念。来到东京国际电影节，花时间观看那些与《巨兽！》、《米亚斯马营的青春性与死》以及《哥斯拉减零》处于同一连续谱系中的电影，实在是一次令人感到谦卑的体验……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "越是仔细审视国际电影真实、有形的世界，人们就越会意识到自己对正在发生的事情其实并没有连贯的概念。来到东京国际电影节，花时间观看那些与《巨兽！》、《米亚斯马营的青春性与死》以及《哥斯拉减零》处于同一连续谱系中的电影，实在是一次令人感到谦卑的体验。很少有哪个单元（如果有的话）能比“亚洲未来”单元更细致地展现亚洲电影的现状与未来走向——该单元汇集了来自远比你预想的更为广阔的国家的10部故事片。当然，影片质量会有所起伏，但那些引人共鸣的作品完全证明了这一展映单元的价值。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“亚洲未来”单元由东京国际电影节资深节目策划、日本电影大学教授兼院长石坂健治负责。尽管他在电影史及其运作机制方面的知识堪称无与伦比，但他却是一位友好而谦逊的访谈对象——随着第39届东京国际电影节的全面展开，他在发掘新锐人才（或在某起悲剧事件中英年早逝的人才）方面的工作正在结出硕果。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "感谢山内悦子（Etsuko Yamanouchi）为访谈提供口译。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《电影舞台》：我已经在影院和电影节资料库里看过了几部“亚洲未来”单元的电影。在西方世界，“亚洲电影”通常只让人联想到少数几个国家——中国、日本、韩国、香港，而东南亚则成了它自己独特的独立类别。但你们的单元呈现了一系列非常多元的电影。在只有10部入选名额的情况下，当你想把亚洲展现为一个比区区几个国家、风格和故事更广阔的宏大图景时，你的考量是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "石坂健治：日本外务省对亚洲的定义相当狭窄——它只包括印度、巴基斯坦、斯里兰卡及以东地区。然而，出于我们自身的一些联系，我们试图在地理和历史上将其进一步向西扩展。因此，我们将西亚以及中东也纳入其中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我可以举一个这种文化联系的例子。比方说伊斯兰文化。它的跨度很广：中心当然在中东，但它经由巴基斯坦延伸至东南亚国家，穿过马来半岛、印度尼西亚，甚至延伸到了菲律宾——棉兰老岛有着非常浓厚的伊斯兰文化。因此，我们决定以这种方式采用我们更广泛的亚洲定义。让我们从相反的角度来看，比如亚文化。日本动漫或漫画一直延伸到了中东，对当地文化产生了影响，这些影响也经常在当地的电影中被提及。由于这些原因，我们决定将所有这些地区都纳入进来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然后你会想到欧洲电影。它们基本上是建立在基督教文化的基础上的。当我想到亚洲，并从更广泛的角度审视亚洲不同文化之间的伊斯兰共性时，我们决定将范围一直延伸到中东是合适的。然而，与欧洲电影或文化的情况不同，当你从语言和宗教的角度来看待亚洲——我所说的这种广义上的亚洲时，在我们对亚洲的定义内部存在着极大的多样性。尽管那里确实存在着某些共性。因此，在选择电影时，我既重视共性，也重视各个国家之间的个体差异。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这很有意思：有时电影节策展人会抵制为单元指定主题。因为当然，所有这些电影都是独立制作的。但主题可能会在不知不觉中浮现。对于今年，你是否注意到这10部来自许多其他国家的电影之间存在着一条显著的贯穿线？我自己看了一些之后，可能也有了一些想法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "嗯，至于我们如何选择界定的区域，我之前已经提过了，但在你观看完所有选定的10部电影之后，确实有些东西可以被视为将它们串联在一起的线索。就今年而言，我们绝对有很多关于家庭剧的电影——父母与孩子之间或兄弟姐妹之间的关系。因此，电影中出现了许多儿童。为什么？我们不知道。但我推测，在这个我们能感觉到可能正在逼近的充满战争与冲突的不稳定时期，人类往往会把目光投向你身边最小的社群，也就是家庭。我不知道这是一个有意识的选择还是无意识的选择，但当你审视这些来自不同国家或地区的10部电影时，这就是我的感受。许多电影都是通过儿童的视角来审视由成年人创造的社会的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在美洲，目前似乎对亚洲电影有着更强的市场和兴趣。很显然，从5年前奉俊昊的奥斯卡获奖，到滨口龙介或毕赣等导演。这似乎是一个非常强劲的时刻。你如何看待这十年中亚洲电影的当前时刻？这是一个特别强劲的时期，还是仍然有一些需要克服的困境？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "嗯，我多少知道你们国家现在是如何看待亚洲电影的。例如，在奥斯卡提名方面，现在的多样性比以前大得多，许多亚洲电影现在都获得了提名，这可能会推动人们对亚洲电影兴趣的增长。我认为亚洲电影仍然有很大的改变空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当谈到美国观众对亚洲电影的兴趣时，我们往往基本上只看东亚国家——包括日本、中国和韩国——然而，随着东南亚国家经济上日益富裕，更大规模的电影正在被制作出来，面向全球发行的发行渠道也在不断发展。所以我认为我们可以期待越来越多的来自这些国家的电影走向世界观众。此外，一些电影导演前往美国并在那里拍片。韩国导演或香港导演长期以来一直在这样做，而且许多国家之间也存在大量合拍片。许多亚洲国家都经历过被殖民的历史。因此，那里有非常非常多的故事可以讲述。所以只要有一个好的制作团队，我确信会有越来越多的好电影从这些国家涌现出来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我欣赏“亚洲未来”单元的一点是，许多电影似乎都是在较小的预算下制作的。我看了切齐扬（Chezhiyan）的《纸花》（Paper Flower），这部电影看起来是用非常简朴的摄影系统拍摄的，但我完全被它迷住了。在进行节目策划时，你怎么看待一位已经拍过长片的导演与一位新锐导演？这会改变你的方法吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "只要我们遵循入选影片必须在导演前三部剧情片之内的规则——我们对此严格遵守——一部电影是导演的处女作、第二部还是第三部，并不会影响我们的选择。我们只看眼前的东西。我刚才提到许多东南亚国家变得更加富裕、正在制作更大规模的电影时，并不是指规模越大就越好。事实上，我经常有相反的感受。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我正想问这个。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "既然我们身处数字时代，你完全可以用低预算拍出一部优秀的电影。我经常在那类小预算作品中发现如宝石般的电影。《纸花》就是这样一个典型案例：一部低预算电影却如此优秀。大多数人听到“印度电影”时，都会联想到宝莱坞类型的电影。事实上，我们选择这部电影是因为我们想向观众展示，印度电影还有不同的类型——不仅仅是宝莱坞。因此我听到一些观众反馈说，他们原本期待一部宝莱坞电影，结果却大感意外并非常享受。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/the-paper-flower-Chezhiyan-1-1200x676.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《纸花》", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我当时还担心你会说他们很失望。我是晚些时候看的，非常赞赏这种精简、安静、克制的风格。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "是的。[笑]嗯，我总是希望选择一部能在日本观众中激起对该国或影片背景人群的尊重的电影。以《纸花》为例。我们可以看到他们通过文学、诗意表达的交流方式，它非常浪漫，但同时又是一部高度知性的电影。你几乎可以在这部电影中看到对印度生活的纪录片式描绘，其中还提及了印度电影制作的历史。如果你是一个印度电影迷，你甚至可以辨认出其中一些曾在其他某部知名电影中出现过的歌曲。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "关于那部电影唯一的遗憾是，导演在7月突然去世了，没能来到这个电影节。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哦，我不知道这件事。太遗憾了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他的妻子[普蕾玛·切齐扬（Prema Chezhiyan）]作为制片人来到了现场。这位导演只拍了两部电影就去世了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "几年前我曾与市山尚三（Ichiyama Shozo）交谈过，他说电影节非常希望有好的评委——而不是那些会倾向于商业作品的好莱坞明星。今年“亚洲未来”单元的评委——两位首席执行官/制片人和一位导演——是一个独特的组合。这背后的考量是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "国际电影节发挥着各种不同的作用。通过邀请人人都想追逐的明星来获取大众媒体的报道，这当然很重要。但对于“亚洲未来”单元，我觉得它的作用是创造一个“公园”，让亚洲电影人与世界各地的其他电影人或制片人等相聚。我们希望为此打造一个大型论坛。出于这个原因，我觉得让大量制片人参与进来也很重要。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如果有的话，你特别看好并对之寄予厚望的亚洲新导演是谁？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是一个难题！[笑]我本来会提到那位已故的《纸花》导演。还有《EDJPOP》的导演卡茨基·弗洛雷斯（Katski Flores）。尽管从某种意义上说这是一部家庭剧，但她通过这部电影传达了非常强烈的政治信息，你能从中了解到过去50年菲律宾历史的如此多内容。我认为能将这两者结合起来对她来说是一个伟大的成就。如你所知，菲律宾现在由费尔南德斯·马科斯的儿子统治，但她没有针对小费尔南德斯·马科斯制作反向评论，而是编织了一个家庭故事来展现这种情绪，这处理得非常巧妙。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "此外，有两位演员转型成为了电影人。纳维德·马哈茂迪[《我真的没什么特别的》（I’m Nothing Special Really）的导演]曾在本电影节[2019年]获得最佳男演员奖。这部电影描绘了伊朗年轻女性的生活。它完全打破了我们通常在关于伊朗女性戴头巾等常规报道中所看到的印象。这些女性根本不戴那些东西，她们喝酒、抽烟——应有尽有。[笑]所以它确实让人耳目一新。这使得这部作品非常特别且富有说服力。而这部哈萨克斯坦电影[《Shyrmauyq》]的导演[阿扎马特·夏尔根（Azamat Shargyn）]是一位非常著名的演员。我当时很好奇他会拍出什么样的一部电影，结果发现它就是哈萨克斯坦的塔可夫斯基。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我不知道你是怎么看《纸花》这一点的——在我看来，《纸花》受到了罗伯特·布列松（Robert Bresson）的影响。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "是的！我注意到这部电影对iPhone的运用非常巧妙、直观。对书本的处理也很有触感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "例如，当他翻动书本时对双手的特写——那太布列松了。更有趣的是其中的新元素，即他运用了来自另一部电影的老歌。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "第39届东京国际电影节将持续至11月4日星期三。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "The closer one looks at the actual, tangible world of international cinema, the more one realizes they have no coherent idea of what is going on. It’s quite humbling to be at the Tokyo International Film Festival and spend time with the films that play on the same continuum as Behemoth! , Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma , and Godzilla Minus Zero . Few (if any) sections offer a more granular view of Asian cinema—where it is, where it might be heading—than Asian Future, which collects ten features from a far wider span of countries than you’d likely anticipate. Quality can, of course, vary, but the titles that resonate entirely justify the showcase."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Asian Future is overseen by Kenji Ishizaka, TIFF’s senior programmer and professor and dean of the Japan Institute of the Moving Image. Though his knowledge of both film history and its practical machinations is essentially unparalleled, he proved a friendly and humble interview subject—someone whose work in collating upcoming talent (or in one tragic case, talent cut short) is bearing fruit as the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival was in full swing."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "My thanks to Etsuko Yamanouchi for providing interpretation."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Film Stage: I’ve seen a handful of films from the Asian Future section now, both in the theater and on the festival library. In the Western world, “Asian cinema” often just suggests a handful of countries—China, Japan, Korea, Hong Kong—and then Southeast Asia becomes its own distinct category. But your section presents a very pluralistic range of films. When you only have 10 films to select, what are your considerations for representing Asia as a much broader picture than just a few countries, styles, and stories?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Kenji Ishizaka : The definition given by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan is quite narrow for the definition of Asia—it only includes up to India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and the east of it. However, we try to expand it further west in terms of geography and history as well, because of certain connections we have. So we include West Asia as well as Middle East."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I’ll give one you example of this cultural connection. Let’s take Islamic culture. It spans a broad band: of course its center is in the Middle East, but it extends through Pakistan into Southeast Asian countries through the Malay Peninsula, Indonesia, and even in the Philippines—Mindanao is very Islamic. So we decided we will use our broader definition of Asia that way. Let’s take the opposite perspective and let’s take subculture. Japanese anime or manga have expanded all the way through the Middle East with its influence on their cultures, which are often referred to in their films as well. For these reasons, we’ve decided to include all this area."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Then you think of European films. They are basically based on Christian culture. When I think of Asia and think of the broader perspective of Islam commonality within different cultures in Asia, we decided that including all the way up to the Middle East would be appropriate. However, unlike the case of European films or cultures, when you look at Asian—this broad definition of Asia I’m talking about—in terms of languages and religions, there is such a variety within our definition of Asia. Although there definitely is some commonality there. So in choosing films, I place importance on both commonality and individual differences among countries."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s interesting: sometimes festival programmers resist assigning a theme to a program. Because of course all these films are made independently. But a theme can unconsciously emerge. For this year, did you notice a significant through line across these 10 films from many other countries? Having seen a handful, I might have some ideas myself."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Well, as for how we choose the defined area, I’ve already mentioned it, but there are certain things you could see as the thread that puts them together after you watch all 10 films that are chosen. In this year’s case, we definitely have many films on family dramas—the relationships between parent and child or among siblings. Therefore there are many children appearing in the films. Why? We don’t know. But I will assume that at this unstable period of wars and conflicts that we feel could be approaching, humans tend to look at the smallest community around you, which is family. I don’t know if it’s a conscious or unconscious choice but when you look at these 10 films across different countries or regions, this is how I feel. Many of the films are made through the perspectives of children looking at the societies created by adults."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In America, there seems to be a much stronger market and interest in Asian cinema at the moment. Obviously Bong Joon-ho’s Oscar wins five years ago to directors like Ryusuke Hamaguchi or Bi Gan. It seems like a very strong moment. How do you feel about this current moment in Asian cinema this decade? Is it a particularly strong time, or are there still struggles that need to be overcome?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Well, I am somewhat aware of how Asian films are now looked at in your country. For instance, for Oscar nominations, there is much more diversity now than before, and many Asian films are now getting nominated, and that would probably propel the growth of interest in Asian films. I think there is still a lot of room for change, still, for Asian films."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When you talk about interest in Asian films on the part of the U.S. audience, we tend to basically look at East Asian countires—including Japan, China, and Korea—however, as Southeast Asian countries are getting more comfortable economically, larger-scale films are getting made, and also the distribution channels are developed for world distribution. So I think we can expect more and more films to come out from these countries for the world audience. Also, some film directors go to the U.S. and make films there. This has been doing quite a bit by Korean directors or directors from Hong Kong for a long time, and there are many co-productions between countries. Many Asian countries have experienced being colonized. Therefore there are many, many stories to be told there. So as long as there’s a good production team, I’m sure there will be more and more good films emerging from such countries."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Something I admire about the Asian Future lineup is that many films seem to be made on smaller budgets. I saw Chezhiyan’s Paper Flower , a film that seemed like it was shot on a very modest camera system, but I was completely taken in by it. When programming, how do you view a director who already has a feature under their belt versus a debut filmmaker? Does that change your approach?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As long as we follow the rule that the film to be chosen has to be within the first three feature films made by the director—which we strictly follow—it doesn’t affect us whether a film is a debut, a second, or third film. We only look at what’s in front of us. When I mentioned earlier that many Southeast Asian countries are getting more affluent, they are making larger scale films, I did not mean that the larger the scale, the better. I, in fact, feel the opposite often."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I was going to ask."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Now that we are in the digital era, you can make an excellent film on a low budget. I often find gem-like films in that kind of small-budget category. Paper Flower is a typical case of that: a low-budget film being so excellent. Most people would imagine Bollywood-type of films when they hear “Indian film.” In fact, we chose this film because we wanted to show the audience there are different types of Indian films—not just Bollywood. So I heard comments from some people in the audience that they were expecting a Bollywood film and they were very pleasantly taken aback and they enjoyed it."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/the-paper-flower-Chezhiyan-1-1200x676.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Paper Flower"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I was worried you’d say they were disappointed. I’d seen it later in the day and something so spare, quiet, contained was very appreciated."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah. article_text:
The closer one looks at the actual, tangible world of international cinema, the more one realizes they have no coherent idea of what is going on. It’s quite humbling to be at the Tokyo International Film Festival and spend time with the films that play on the same continuum as Behemoth! , Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma , and Godzilla Minus Zero . Few (if any) sections offer a more granular view of Asian cinema—where it is, where it might be heading—than Asian Future, which collects ten features from a far wider span of countries than you’d likely anticipate. Quality can, of course, vary, but the titles that resonate entirely justify the showcase.

Asian Future is overseen by Kenji Ishizaka, TIFF’s senior programmer and professor and dean of the Japan Institute of the Moving Image. Though his knowledge of both film history and its practical machinations is essentially unparalleled, he proved a friendly and humble interview subject—someone whose work in collating upcoming talent (or in one tragic case, talent cut short) is bearing fruit as the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival was in full swing.

My thanks to Etsuko Yamanouchi for providing interpretation.

The Film Stage: I’ve seen a handful of films from the Asian Future section now, both in the theater and on the festival library. In the Western world, “Asian cinema” often just suggests a handful of countries—China, Japan, Korea, Hong Kong—and then Southeast Asia becomes its own distinct category. But your section presents a very pluralistic range of films. When you only have 10 films to select, what are your considerations for representing Asia as a much broader picture than just a few countries, styles, and stories?

Kenji Ishizaka : The definition given by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan is quite narrow for the definition of Asia—it only includes up to India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and the east of it. However, we try to expand it further west in terms of geography and history as well, because of certain connections we have. So we include West Asia as well as Middle East.

I’ll give one you example of this cultural connection. Let’s take Islamic culture. It spans a broad band: of course its center is in the Middle East, but it extends through Pakistan into Southeast Asian countries through the Malay Peninsula, Indonesia, and even in the Philippines—Mindanao is very Islamic. So we decided we will use our broader definition of Asia that way. Let’s take the opposite perspective and let’s take subculture. Japanese anime or manga have expanded all the way through the Middle East with its influence on their cultures, which are often referred to in their films as well. For these reasons, we’ve decided to include all this area.

Then you think of European films. They are basically based on Christian culture. When I think of Asia and think of the broader perspective of Islam commonality within different cultures in Asia, we decided that including all the way up to the Middle East would be appropriate. However, unlike the case of European films or cultures, when you look at Asian—this broad definition of Asia I’m talking about—in terms of languages and religions, there is such a variety within our definition of Asia. Although there definitely is some commonality there. So in choosing films, I place importance on both commonality and individual differences among countries.

It’s interesting: sometimes festival programmers resist assigning a theme to a program. Because of course all these films are made independently. But a theme can unconsciously emerge. For this year, did you notice a significant through line across these 10 films from many other countries? Having seen a handful, I might have some ideas myself.

Well, as for how we choose the defined area, I’ve already mentioned it, but there are certain things you could see as the thread that puts them together after you watch all 10 films that are chosen. In this year’s case, we definitely have many films on family dramas—the relationships between parent and child or among siblings. Therefore there are many children appearing in the films. Why? We don’t know. But I will assume that at this unstable period of wars and conflicts that we feel could be approaching, humans tend to look at the smallest community around you, which is family. I don’t know if it’s a conscious or unconscious choice but when you look at these 10 films across different countries or regions, this is how I feel. Many of the films are made through the perspectives of children looking at the societies created by adults.

In America, there seems to be a much stronger market and interest in Asian cinema at the moment. Obviously Bong Joon-ho’s Oscar wins five years ago to directors like Ryusuke Hamaguchi or Bi Gan. It seems like a very strong moment. How do you feel about this current moment in Asian cinema this decade? Is it a particularly strong time, or are there still struggles that need to be overcome?

Well, I am somewhat aware of how Asian films are now looked at in your country. For instance, for Oscar nominations, there is much more diversity now than before, and many Asian films are now getting nominated, and that would probably propel the growth of interest in Asian films. I think there is still a lot of room for change, still, for Asian films.

When you talk about interest in Asian films on the part of the U.S. audience, we tend to basically look at East Asian countires—including Japan, China, and Korea—however, as Southeast Asian countries are getting more comfortable economically, larger-scale films are getting made, and also the distribution channels are developed for world distribution. So I think we can expect more and more films to come out from these countries for the world audience. Also, some film directors go to the U.S. and make films there. This has been doing quite a bit by Korean directors or directors from Hong Kong for a long time, and there are many co-productions between countries. Many Asian countries have experienced being colonized. Therefore there are many, many stories to be told there. So as long as there’s a good production team, I’m sure there will be more and more good films emerging from such countries.

Something I admire about the Asian Future lineup is that many films seem to be made on smaller budgets. I saw Chezhiyan’s Paper Flower , a film that seemed like it was shot on a very modest camera system, but I was completely taken in by it. When programming, how do you view a director who already has a feature under their belt versus a debut filmmaker? Does that change your approach?

As long as we follow the rule that the film to be chosen has to be within the first three feature films made by the director—which we strictly follow—it doesn’t affect us whether a film is a debut, a second, or third film. We only look at what’s in front of us. When I mentioned earlier that many Southeast Asian countries are getting more affluent, they are making larger scale films, I did not mean that the larger the scale, the better. I, in fact, feel the opposite often.

I was going to ask.

Now that we are in the digital era, you can make an excellent film on a low budget. I often find gem-like films in that kind of small-budget category. Paper Flower is a typical case of that: a low-budget film being so excellent. Most people would imagine Bollywood-type of films when they hear “Indian film.” In fact, we chose this film because we wanted to show the audience there are different types of Indian films—not just Bollywood. So I heard comments from some people in the audience that they were expecting a Bollywood film and they were very pleasantly taken aback and they enjoyed it.

The Paper Flower

I was worried you’d say they were disappointed. I’d seen it later in the day and something so spare, quiet, contained was very appreciated.

Yeah. [Laughs] Well, I always want to choose a film that would evoke respect for that country or the people where the film comes from among the audience in Japan. So let’s take Paper Flower . We could see their way of communication through literature, poetry, and it’s very romantic, but at the same time a highly intelligent film. You could almost see a documentary-like depiction of life in India in that film, and there’s some reference to the history of Indian filmmaking. If you’re a cinephile of Indian films, you could distinguish some songs that were used in another certain well-known film, for example.

The only regrettable thing about that film is that the director passed away suddenly in July and couldn’t come to this festival.

Oh, I didn’t know that. That’s terrible.

His wife [Prema Chezhiyan] acted as the producer and she came. The director only shot two films and passed away.

A couple of years ago I spoke with Ichiyama Shozo, and he said that TIFF really wants good jury members—not Hollywood stars who will gravitate to something commercial. The Asian Future jury this year—two CEO/producers and one director—is a unique combination. What was the thought process behind that?

There are various roles international film festivals play. Of course it’s important to have the reports by mass media by having stars that everybody gravitates towards. But for the Asian Future section, I feel its role is to create a “park” where Asian filmmakers meet with other filmmakers or producers, etc of the world. We want to create a big forum for that. So for that reason, I feel it’s important to involve lots of producers as well.

Who, if anybody, is a new Asian director you’re particularly excited about and you expect great things from?

Tough question! [Laughs] I would’ve mentioned the director who passed away, of Paper Flower . The director of EDJPOP , Katski Flores. Although it’s, in a way, a family drama, she gives a very strong political message through that film, and you could learn so much about the last 50 years of Filipino history. I think to combine the two was a great feat for her. As you know, the Philippines are now ruled by the son of Fernando Marcos, but instead of making anti-comment against Fernando Marcos Jr, she wove a family story to show that sentiment, and that was very skillfully done.

Also, two actors became filmmakers. Navid Mahmoudi [director of I’m Nothing Special Really ] won the best actor award at this festival [in 2019]. And this film depicts the life of young women in Iran. It just is the opposite of what we see in regular reports about Iranian women with hijab and so on. These women are not wearing anything like that and they’re drinking and smoking—you name it. [Laughs] So it really takes the wool away from your eyes. That makes this title very special and eloquent. And this director [Azamat Shargyn] of this Kazakhstan film [ Shyrmauyq ] is a very well-known actor. I was wondering what kind of film he would make, and it turned out to be Tarkovsky in Kazakhstan.

I don’t know how you felt about this aspect of Paper Flower —to me, Paper Flower was influenced by Robert Bresson.

Yes! I noted how the film has a very smart, intuitive depiction of iPhones. The handling of the books was very tactile, too.

The close-ups on hands when he was handling the book, for example—that was so Bresson-like. What made it more interesting was the new element, in that he utilized the old song from another film.

The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival continues until Wednesday, November 4.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Sony Pictures has pre-emptively bought Penthouse , an original idea by Drew Pearce , with Tom Holland ’s production company Billy17 and Pearce’s Point Of No Return producing. The film is being developed as a starring vehicle for Holland.

Pearce ( The Thomas Crown Affair, The Fall Guy, Iron Man 3 ) will be writing the script, with Holland and his Billy17 partners playing an instrumental role in its development alongside Pearce.

Related Stories

Callan Farris, Lexi Minetree & Josh Macqueen Round Out Cast Of Sony Comedy ‘Narcs’

Sony’s Screen Gems Sets YouTube Exec Fede Goldenberg To Top Genre Label; Ashley Brucks Segues To Producer Role

The plot is under wraps, but Penthouse described as a thriller. Tom Holland, Harry Holland and Will South will produce on behalf of Billy17 alongside Pearce on behalf of Point of Not Return. Ian Fisher will executive produce for Point of No Return.

Following the record-breaking success of Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Penthouse builds on the already strong relationship between Sony and Holland, whose Billy17 has a producing deal with Sony Pictures. Holland is still on screens with Sony Pictures’ Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which counts a worldwide gross of more than $2 billion.

Watch on Deadline

Holland will also star in Sony Pictures’ upcoming film about Fred Astaire, which recently announced Margaret Qualley, Sabrina Carpenter and Talia Ryder as co-stars; Holland and Billy17 also serve as producers of the pic.

Additionally, Holland recently starred in The Odyssey. He is repped by WME and Sloane Offer.

Pearce’s writing credits include Fast & Furious Presents: Hobbs & Shaw and Hotel Artemis, which he also directed. The Thomas Crown Affair , starring and directed by Michael B. Jordan, hits theaters in March 2027. Pearce is repped by WME and Sloane Offer.
